findings.title: English reference file path is computed with a regex that does not match real locale suffixes, causing the verifier to fail or compare against the wrong file
findings.body: The English bundle path is derived with `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. The character class `[a-zA-Z-_]` does not include digits, so locale suffixes containing digits such as `_zh_CN`, `_zh_TW`, `_pt_BR` are not matched and the path is left unchanged (pointing at the translated file itself). Additionally, for files already named `messages_en.properties` the regex matches `_en` and rewrites it to `_en.properties` (harmless), but for any file whose locale suffix contains a digit the verifier will read the translated file as the 'English' source. Consequence: the HTML policy decision (`containsHtml(englishValue)`) is made against the translated value instead of the English source, so translations can be wrongly allowed or wrongly rejected, and the anchor-tag comparison compares a translation against itself. The regex should be something like `_[a-zA-Z]{2}(_[A-Za-z0-9]+)?\\.properties` or, more robustly, the locale should be parsed from the file name.

findings.title: Missing English properties file causes an uncaught RuntimeException instead of a proper verification message
findings.body: When the computed English file does not exist (which, per the path bug above, happens for every locale whose suffix contains digits, and also for any key present only in a translation), `new FileInputStream(englishFile)` throws FileNotFoundException which is wrapped in a `RuntimeException` and propagates out of `verify()`. `verify()` only catches `IOException` around `Files.readString`, so this RuntimeException escapes the declared `MojoExecutionException` contract and will crash the build with a stack trace rather than reporting a verification problem. The English bundle load should tolerate a missing file (treat as empty bundle, as `getEnglishValue` already does for missing keys) or report a proper message.

findings.title: Anchor sanitization removes the English anchor from the translated value at the wrong position and can loop forever / corrupt the value
findings.body: `santizeAnchors` iterates over anchors in the translated value and, for each match, calls `value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")`. `replaceFirst` removes the first occurrence of the English anchor text anywhere in the translated string, not the occurrence at the translated matcher's position. If the translated value contains the same anchor text earlier (e.g. repeated links, or text identical to the tag), the wrong occurrence is removed and the remaining anchors shift, so subsequent iterations compare mismatched anchors and report false 'Didn't find anchor tag' errors. It also mutates `value` while iterating with a Matcher created from the original string, which can cause the loop to never terminate or to skip anchors when the removal shortens the string (Matcher indices become stale). The method should rebuild the string by removing the exact matched region (e.g. using `matcher.start()/end()` with a StringBuilder) instead of `replaceFirst` on the whole value.

findings.title: HTML detection regex only matches lowercase single-word tags, so uppercase or attribute-bearing tags in the English source disable HTML allowance for translations
findings.body:
`HTML_TAGS = Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")` is used by `containsHtml` to decide whether the English source contains HTML and therefore whether `POLICY_SOME_HTML` (allowing br/p/strong/b) is applied to the translation. The pattern requires the tag name to start with a lowercase letter and contain only lowercase letters, so English values containing uppercase tags (`
`, `

`), self-closing or attribute forms like `
` (actually matched by `[^>]*` after `br`, but `
` is not), or tags with uppercase names will be classified as 'no HTML'. A translation that legitimately mirrors an uppercase English tag (e.g. `
`) would then be sanitized with `POLICY_NO_HTML`, stripping the tag and producing a false 'Illegal HTML' failure. The pattern should be case-insensitive (`Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE`) and should match the tags actually allowed by the policy.

findings.title: HTML policy allows only br/p/strong/b but the verifier's anchor handling strips <a> tags before sanitization, so the check does not actually validate that translations only use the allowed elements
findings.body: `POLICY_SOME_HTML` allows only `br`, `p`, `strong`, `b`, yet `santizeAnchors` removes anchor tags from the translated value before `policy.sanitize(value)` runs (line 88 runs before line 92). This means an `<a href="javascript:...">` or any other anchor in a translation is never seen by the sanitizer: it is either silently removed (when it matches the English anchor) or reported only as 'Didn't find anchor tag' (when it doesn't). The sanitizer therefore never validates the attributes of anchors that translations are allowed to contain (email templates legitimately contain `<a href="{0}">`), and a translation containing a malicious anchor that happens to textually match the English anchor is accepted without any attribute checking. The anchor handling should instead let the sanitizer process the value with a policy that allows `a` with safe URL schemes (e.g. `allowAttributes("href").matching(...)` on the policy), and only afterwards compare the surviving anchors with the English ones.

findings.title: Unconditional unescapeHtml4 on the sanitized value corrupts legitimate HTML entities in message values
findings.body: After sanitizing, the code unconditionally applies `StringEscapeUtils.unescapeHtml4(sanitized)` (line 95) and also unescapes the original value in `normalizeValue` (line 130). The OWASP sanitizer escapes text content (e.g. `&` becomes `&`, `'` becomes `'`), and the comparison then unescapes both sides. However, unescaping the sanitized output also unescapes entities that were present verbatim in the source value and were intentionally double-escaped by the sanitizer, and it will turn a literal `&amp;` in the source into `&` on both sides, masking real differences. More importantly, a value that legitimately contains the text `<script>` (escaped HTML shown to the user) is unescaped to `<script>` on the value side, then re-sanitized... actually the sanitize happens before unescape, so the unescape happens after sanitize and can reintroduce `<` characters into `sanitized` that are then compared against the unescaped original; any value whose sanitized form differs only by entity encoding will be compared after both sides are unescaped, which can both hide real differences (a translation that adds `<` where English has `<`) and create false positives. The unescape should only be applied to compensate for the sanitizer's own escaping of characters that were not entities in the source, not as a blanket unescape of the whole string.

findings.title: templateHelp normalization regex only strips uppercase claim names, leaving lowercase or mixed-case placeholders to fail verification
findings.body: `normalizeValue` special-cases the key `templateHelp` with `value.replaceAll("CLAIM\\.<[A-Z]*>", "")`. The comment says it allows `CLAIM.<NAME>`, but the regex only matches uppercase letters. A translation using `CLAIM.<name>` or `CLAIM.<sub>` (lowercase claim names are common, e.g. the zh_CN admin message references `${CLAIM.sub}`) will not be stripped, the `<name>` will be treated as an HTML tag by the sanitizer, and the verifier will report a false 'Illegal HTML' error. The regex should be case-insensitive or match any non-`>` characters: `CLAIM\\.<[^>]*>`.

findings.title: Choice-format normalization regex does not handle nested braces, breaking verification of messages with nested choice/format patterns
findings.body: For keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit` and `error-invalid-multivalued-size`, the code replaces `\{[0-9]+,choice,[^}]*}` with `...`. The character class `[^}]*` stops at the first `}`, so a choice pattern containing a nested brace (e.g. `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<{2,number}}` or the new `error-invalid-multivalued-size` value `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` combined with other placeholders on the same line) will only be partially replaced, leaving a dangling `{` or `}` that the sanitizer treats as text and that will mismatch the sanitized output, producing false 'Illegal HTML' reports. The replacement should consume balanced braces or the whole `{n,choice,...}` construct including nested groups.

findings.title: Tests for HTML verification rely on an English fixture that the buggy path computation never actually locates, so the tests do not exercise the intended code path
findings.body: The new tests load fixtures from the classpath (e.g. `illegalHtmlTag_en.properties`, `noHtml_de.properties` + `noHtml_en.properties`). `VerifyMessageProperties` computes the English file path from the translated file's absolute path using `replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. The test resources live under `target/test-classes` (or `src/test/resources`), which contains neither `resources-community` nor a `resources` directory, so for `noHtml_de.properties` the computed 'English' path is `.../noHtml_en.properties` only if the regex matches `_de` — it does match `_de`, so the fixture works by accident. But the tests never cover a locale with digits (e.g. `zh_CN`), never cover a file in a `resources-community` tree, and never cover the case where the English file is missing. As a result the path-computation bug (finding #1) and the missing-file crash (finding #2) are not caught. Tests should include a fixture pair with a digit-containing locale and a test for a translation whose English file does not exist.

findings.title: Lithuanian email HTML bodies had corrupted href attributes (`href=LT"{0}"`) which the PR fixes, but the same corruption pattern indicates a prior bad edit; verify no other files have it

findings.title: Account UI error-invalid-multivalued-size changed from {{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}} (i18next interpolation) to {0}/{1}/{2} with a MessageFormat choice pattern, which i18next will not interpolate correctly

findings.title: Chinese admin templateHelp still contains a full-width space inside `<NAME >` that the verifier's templateHelp normalization does not strip
findings.body: The diff changes `CLAIM.<NAME >` to `CLAIM.<NAME>` (removing a full-width/ideographic space U+3000 that was inside the angle brackets). The original zh_CN value had `CLAIM.<NAME\u3000>` (with an ideographic space before `>`), which the regex would not match, so the verifier would have flagged it. findings.title: owasp-java-html-sanitizer 20240325.1 is used without a stated policy for URL schemes on allowed elements; combined with the anchor-stripping logic this leaves anchor validation entirely to string comparison
findings.body: The PR adds `com.googlecode.owasp-java-html-sanitizer:owasp-java-html-sanitizer:20240325.1` to verify message HTML. The `POLICY_SOME_HTML` policy allows `br`, `p`, `strong`, `b` with no attributes and no URL policy, and `POLICY_NO_HTML` allows nothing. Because `santizeAnchors` removes all `<a>` tags from the value before sanitization (see the anchor finding), the sanitizer never gets the chance to validate `href` values (e.g. reject `javascript:` URLs) in translations. The version 20240325.1 is recent enough, but the design means the sanitizer dependency is effectively only used to strip non-whitelisted tags, and all anchor safety relies on exact string equality with the English source. If a translation's anchor matches the English anchor textually, its `href` is never checked by the sanitizer. The policy should allow `a` with `href` restricted to safe schemes (e.g. `allowAttributes("href").matching(uris().withSchemes("http","https","mailto"))`) and the anchor comparison should happen after sanitization.

findings.title: Difference-highlighting substring logic can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when one string is a prefix of the other
findings.body: When `sanitized` and `value` differ, the code computes `start` as the length of the common prefix and `end` as the length of the common suffix, then calls `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` and `sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end)`. If one string is a strict prefix of the other (e.g. value = 'abc', sanitized = 'abcd'), then start = 3 and end = 0, and `value.substring(3, 3)` is fine, but if the strings share both a prefix and a suffix that overlap (e.g. value = 'aa', sanitized = 'a'), start can exceed `value.length() - end`, causing `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` (begin > end). Example: value = 'aba', sanitized = 'aa': common prefix 'a' (start=1), common suffix 'a' (end=1), then `value.substring(1, 3-1=2)` = 'b' and `sanitized.substring(1, 2-1=1)` → begin 1 > end 1 is OK (empty), but value='aa', sanitized='a': start=1, end=1, `sanitized.substring(1, 1-1=0)` → begin 1 > end 0 → StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The verifier would crash with an unhelpful exception instead of reporting the illegal HTML. The code should clamp `start`/`end` so that `start + end <= min(value.length(), sanitized.length())`.

findings.title: Email RTL style stripping uses a hardcoded English attribute string that will not match translations that reorder or translate the style attribute
findings.body: `normalizeValue` strips ` style="direction: rtl;"` (with an English attribute name and value) from values in files whose path contains 'email'. The OWASP sanitizer would otherwise escape or strip the `style` attribute (it is not allowed by either policy), causing a false 'Illegal HTML' report for RTL email templates. However, the strip is a literal string match: any translation that writes the attribute differently (e.g. `style='direction: rtl;'`, `style="direction:rtl;"`, or with extra spaces) will not be stripped and will false-positive. More importantly, the check `file.getAbsolutePath().contains("email")` is a heuristic on the path; the same RTL style may legitimately appear in non-email themes. The normalization should use a regex tolerant of quoting/spacing, or better, the policy should allow the `style` attribute with a strict `direction: rtl` value matcher for email templates.

findings.title: Czech error-invalid-multivalued-size choice pattern uses an incomplete set of plural forms

This is actually a reasonable Czech plural mapping (0 and 5+ use genitive plural 'hodnot', 1 uses accusative singular 'hodnotu', 2-4 use nominative plural 'hodnoty'). However, the English source uses `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` — the choice is on `{2}` (the maximum), not `{1}` (the minimum). The Czech translation attaches a choice to `{1}` as well, which diverges from the English structure and will produce grammatically correct but structurally different output. findings.title: changedAnchor test fixture has no trailing newline and the English fixture does, which may affect PropertyResourceBundle parsing edge cases but is not itself a defect; however the test only covers a changed href, not a changed tag structure
findings.body: The `changedAnchor_de.properties` fixture ends without a newline (`\ No newline at end of file`) while `changedAnchor_en.properties` also has no trailing newline. The test `verifyNoChangedAnchors` checks that a translation with `<a href="http://malicious.com">` against an English `<a href="http://example.com">` produces 'Didn't find anchor tag'. This covers the changed-href case. It does not cover: (a) a translation with an extra anchor not present in English, (b) a translation missing an anchor present in English, (c) a translation with a self-closing or differently-structured anchor. The `santizeAnchors` loop breaks on the first mismatch, so case (a) with multiple anchors where the first matches but the second doesn't is partially covered, but case (b) (missing anchor) is not tested at all — a translation that drops an anchor entirely will pass `santizeAnchors` silently (the while loop simply doesn't execute for the missing anchor) and then the sanitizer will not complain because there is no extra HTML. A missing anchor in a translation is a real defect (broken link) that the verifier should catch but currently does not. This is a functional gap in the new verifier.

findings.title: Verifier does not detect translations that omit an anchor tag present in the English source
findings.body: `santizeAnchors` only iterates over anchors found in the *translated* value (`matcher = ANCHOR_PATTERN.matcher(value)`) and checks each against the English anchors. If a translation simply omits an `<a>` tag that exists in the English source (e.g. the English has two links and the translation has only one), the loop runs once for the single translated anchor, matches it against the first English anchor, removes it, and returns without ever noticing that the second English anchor has no counterpart. The subsequent sanitization also passes because there is no extra HTML in the translation. The result is a silently broken translation (missing link) that the verifier — whose stated purpose is to catch changed anchors — does not report. The method should also iterate over the English anchors and verify each has a matching counterpart in the translation (i.e. compare counts and sequences in both directions).

findings.title: verify() catches only IOException from Files.readString but verifySafeHtml() throws RuntimeException for file read errors, breaking the declared exception contract
findings.body: `verify()` declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and wraps `IOException` from `Files.readString` into `MojoExecutionException`. However, `verifySafeHtml()` (called inside the try block) catches `IOException` from the two `FileInputStream` constructions and rethrows them as `RuntimeException` (lines 70 and 79). These RuntimeExceptions are not caught by the `catch (IOException e)` block and propagate out of `verify()` as unchecked exceptions. The caller (presumably a Maven Mojo) expects `MojoExecutionException` for verification failures; a `RuntimeException` will produce an unhandled stack trace. The `verifySafeHtml` method should either declare `throws MojoExecutionException` and throw that, or `verify()` should catch `RuntimeException` from `verifySafeHtml` and wrap it.

findings.title: PropertyResourceBundle is created with the platform default charset instead of UTF-8, which can misread non-ASCII translations
findings.body: `new PropertyResourceBundle(fis)` uses the constructor `PropertyResourceBundle(InputStream)` which, per the JavaDoc, reads the stream as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1). Keycloak's message properties files are UTF-8 (the project sets `project.build.sourceEncoding=UTF-8` and modern Keycloak loads properties as UTF-8). Reading a UTF-8 file as ISO-8859-1 will mojibake all non-ASCII characters (e.g. Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic), which means the sanitizer operates on corrupted text and the comparison against the sanitized form may produce false 'Illegal HTML' reports for any translation containing non-ASCII characters (the mojibake bytes may include characters that look like HTML entities or tags after unescapeHtml4). The code should use `new PropertyResourceBundle(new InputStreamReader(fis, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))` to match Keycloak's actual loading behavior.

This is the primary bundle being verified, so all non-ASCII translations are mojibake'd before sanitization and comparison. This is a critical correctness bug for the verifier's stated purpose (verifying translated message resources). The fix is to wrap the InputStream in an InputStreamReader with UTF-8.

findings.title: Test for duplicate keys was changed from contains() to hasItem() but the assertion semantics changed subtly
findings.body: The original test used `Matchers.contains(Matchers.containsString("Duplicate keys in file"))` which asserts the list has exactly one element matching. The new test uses `Matchers.hasItem(Matchers.containsString("Duplicate keys in file"))` which asserts the list has at least one matching element. The change is reasonable (the verifier may produce multiple messages), but the test no longer verifies that the duplicate-keys message is the *only* message or that it appears exactly once. This is a minor weakening of the test, not a defect.

findings.title: Renamed duplicate-keys fixture is now an English file, but the verifier's HTML check will also run on it and may produce additional messages
findings.body: The fixture was renamed from `duplicate_keys.properties` to `duplicateKeys_en.properties`. Because the file is now named `*_en.properties`, the verifier's `verifySafeHtml` will compute the English path from itself (the regex rewrites `_en` to `_en`), load itself as the English bundle, and run the HTML check on the value `value` (no HTML). The duplicate-keys check will produce one message, and the HTML check will produce none. The test asserts `hasItem(containsString("Duplicate keys in file"))`, which passes. However, the test no longer isolates the duplicate-keys check from the HTML check; if the HTML check were to produce a message for this fixture (it doesn't, since 'value' has no HTML), the test would still pass. This is fine but the fixture name change means the test now also exercises the HTML path implicitly. Not a defect, just a note.

findings.title: Special-case key matching uses exact string equality for 'templateHelp' and 'optimizeLookupHelp' and startsWith for 'linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit', but the same keys may appear in different message bundles (login, admin, account, email) with different surrounding text
findings.body: The `normalizeValue` method special-cases keys by exact name (`templateHelp`, `optimizeLookupHelp`) or prefix (`linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit`). These keys exist in multiple bundles (e.g. `templateHelp` in admin messages, `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit.*` in email messages). The special-casing is applied regardless of which bundle the file belongs to, which is correct since the key names are globally unique. However, the special-case for `error-invalid-multivalued-size` is also applied, and this key exists in login, admin, and account bundles. The normalization strips the choice pattern from the value before sanitization, which is correct for the FreeMarker themes but means the verifier does not actually validate the choice pattern syntax (a malformed choice pattern would be stripped and not checked). This is a deliberate trade-off, not a defect, but it means the verifier cannot catch broken MessageFormat patterns in these keys.

findings.title: Removal of '<!-- -->' comments assumes the sanitizer inserts them only for double curly braces, but this may also remove legitimate comment-like text
findings.body: The code does `sanitized = sanitized.replace("<!-- -->", "")` with the comment 'Sanitizer will add them when there are double curly braces'. The OWASP sanitizer, when it encounters text that looks like an HTML comment or certain constructs, may insert `<!-- -->` as a placeholder. However, if a message value legitimately contains the literal text `<!-- -->` (e.g. documentation about HTML comments), the sanitizer would escape it to `<!-- -->`, and then `unescapeHtml4` would turn it back into `<!-- -->`, and then the `replace` would remove it, causing a false mismatch (the original value had `<!-- -->`, the sanitized+unescaped+replaced value has it removed). This is an edge case, but the blanket removal is fragile. The removal should only happen if the original value did not contain `<!-- -->`.

findings.title: ANCHOR_PATTERN `</?a[^>]*>` matches any tag starting with 'a' (e.g. `<article>`, `<abbr>`), not just anchor tags
findings.body: The pattern `</?a[^>]*>` matches `<a...>` and `</a...>` but also matches `<article>`, `<abbr>`, `<address>`, etc., because `[^>]*` allows any characters after the initial `a`. If a translation legitimately contains an `<article>` or `<abbr>` tag (unlikely in Keycloak messages, but possible in future), the anchor sanitization would treat it as an anchor and try to match it against English anchors, producing a false 'Didn't find anchor tag' error. The pattern should be `</?a(\s[^>]*)?>` or `</?a[\s>]` to ensure the tag name is exactly `a`.

findings.title: HTML_TAGS pattern `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` does not match tags with uppercase letters or digits in the tag name (e.g. `<h1>`, `<H1>`)
findings.body:
The pattern `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` requires the tag name to consist only of lowercase letters. HTML tags like `

`, `

` (headings), `` (unlikely), or uppercase tags `
`, `

` will not match. If an English message contains `

`, `containsHtml` returns false, and the translation is checked with `POLICY_NO_HTML`, so a translation that mirrors the `

` would be falsely rejected. The pattern should be `<[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*[^>]*>` or use `Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE` with `<[a-z]+[0-9]*[^>]*>`.

findings.title: HTML policy decision is based solely on whether the English source contains a lowercase HTML tag; a translation can introduce HTML that the English source does not have, and the verifier only catches it if the English source happens to contain a matching lowercase tag
findings.body:
The policy selection `containsHtml(englishValue) ? POLICY_SOME_HTML : POLICY_NO_HTML` means: if the English source has no HTML (or has HTML that the regex doesn't detect, e.g. uppercase tags), the translation is checked with `POLICY_NO_HTML`, which strips ALL HTML. This is the intended behavior (translations should not add HTML that English doesn't have). However, if the English source contains HTML that the regex misses (uppercase tags, tags with digits like `

`), the translation is checked with `POLICY_NO_HTML` even though the English source legitimately contains HTML, and a translation that mirrors the English HTML would be falsely rejected. Conversely, if the English source contains HTML, the translation is allowed `br/p/strong/b` — but the English source might contain `` tags (which are stripped by `santizeAnchors` before sanitization), so the translation could contain `` tags that match the English anchors and pass, but also could contain `` tags that the English source doesn't have (the English source might only have `` tags), and the verifier would allow them because `POLICY_SOME_HTML` allows `b`. This means a translation can add ``, ``, `

`, `
` tags that the English source does not have, and the verifier will not flag them. The policy should be derived from the actual set of tags present in the English source, not a binary 'has HTML' check.

findings.title: santizeAnchors is called on the translated value but the English value is not sanitized for anchors, so the comparison is asymmetric
findings.body:
`santizeAnchors(key, value, englishValue)` removes matching anchors from the translated `value` but does not remove them from `englishValue`. The English value is only used for the `containsHtml` check and the anchor matching. This asymmetry means: (a) the English value's anchors are not stripped before `containsHtml`, so if the English value contains ONLY anchors (e.g. `link`), `containsHtml` returns true (the regex `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` matches ``), and `POLICY_SOME_HTML` is selected — which allows `br/p/strong/b` but NOT `a`. So a translation that mirrors the English anchors would have its anchors stripped by `santizeAnchors` (matching the English anchors), and then the remaining text is sanitized with `POLICY_SOME_HTML` (which doesn't allow `a`, but there are no `a` tags left). This works by accident. But if the English value contains anchors AND other HTML (e.g. `

link

`), `containsHtml` returns true, `POLICY_SOME_HTML` is selected, the translation's anchors are stripped, and the remaining `

` tags are allowed. This is correct. The asymmetry is intentional (only the translation's anchors need to be removed for the sanitizer), but it means the English value's anchors are never validated by the sanitizer — if the English source itself contains a malicious anchor (e.g. ``), the verifier would not catch it because the English value is never sanitized. The verifier should also sanitize the English value (or at least validate its anchors) to catch malicious English source messages.

findings.title: PropertyResourceBundle is loaded for every file, but the English bundle is loaded once per translated file, causing O(n) file reads for n translations
findings.body: For each translated properties file, `verifySafeHtml` loads the English bundle from disk (line 76). If there are 30 translations of the same bundle, the English file is read 30 times. This is inefficient but not a correctness issue for a build-time verifier. The English bundle could be cached per directory/bundle name. Minor performance point.

findings.title: VerifyMessageProperties instance fields (messages, file) are not thread-safe; if the Mojo runs verifications in parallel, shared state would be corrupted
findings.body: The class has instance fields `file` and `messages` (line 39-40). `messages` is initialized in `verify()` (line 47) and appended to in `verifySafeHtml` and `verifyNoDuplicateKeys`. If a single `VerifyMessageProperties` instance is used from multiple threads (e.g. a parallel Maven build), the `messages` list would be corrupted. However, the class is instantiated per file (the test does `new VerifyMessageProperties(file)`), so each file has its own instance. If the Mojo creates one instance per file and processes files in parallel, each instance is independent and thread-safe. If the Mojo reuses a single instance for multiple files, `messages` would accumulate across files and `file` would be overwritten. The class should either be immutable (pass file to constructor, return messages from verify) or documented as not thread-safe. Currently `file` is final but `messages` is mutable instance state, which is a code smell.

findings.title: Field 'messages' is mutable instance state initialized in verify(); should be a local variable returned by verify()
findings.body: `messages` is declared as an instance field (line 40) but is only used within `verify()` and its callees. It is initialized at the start of `verify()` (line 47) and returned at the end. Making it an instance field means the object holds state between calls, and calling `verify()` twice on the same instance would accumulate messages from both calls (since `messages = new ArrayList<>()` reinitializes it, this is actually safe). However, the field is unnecessary; it could be a local variable in `verify()` passed to the helper methods, or the helper methods could return their messages. Minor design point.

findings.title: getEnglishValue returns empty string for missing keys, which makes containsHtml return false and POLICY_NO_HTML apply, potentially rejecting translations that add HTML for keys missing in English
findings.body: `getEnglishValue` catches `MissingResourceException` and returns `""`. If a key exists in a translation but not in the English bundle (a common situation for community translations that add keys before the English source is updated), `englishValue` is empty, `containsHtml("")` returns false, and `POLICY_NO_HTML` is applied. If the translation contains HTML (e.g. a link), the sanitizer strips it and the verifier reports 'Illegal HTML'. This is arguably correct behavior (translations should not add HTML for keys that don't exist in English), but it means a translation that adds a new key with HTML will always fail verification until the English source adds the same key with HTML. The verifier should perhaps warn differently for keys missing in English (e.g. 'Key X exists in translation but not in English source') rather than treating it as 'no HTML allowed'.

findings.title: Anchor mismatch message does not include the file name, making it hard to locate the problem
findings.body: When `santizeAnchors` finds an anchor in the translation that doesn't match the English source, it adds the message `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string"` (line 157). Unlike the 'Illegal HTML' message (line 111) which includes the key and file, this message does not include the key or the file name. In a build with hundreds of files, the developer would have to search for the anchor text across all files to find the offending translation. The message should include the key and file, e.g. `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string for key " + key + " in file " + file`.

findings.title: Duplicate keys message includes the absolute file path, which leaks build machine paths into CI logs
findings.body: The duplicate-keys message (line 194) includes `file.getAbsolutePath()`. Absolute paths in CI logs can leak information about the build environment (user names, directory structures). The 'Illegal HTML' message (line 111) uses `file` (which calls `toString()` on the File, returning the path — also potentially absolute depending on how the File was constructed). For consistency and to avoid leaking absolute paths, both messages should use a relative path or just the file name. Minor, but a common CI hygiene concern.

findings.title: 'Illegal HTML' message includes the full File object (toString) which may be an absolute path

Same concern as the duplicate-keys message. Should use a relative path or file name for consistency and to avoid leaking build paths.

findings.title: Test helper getFile uses File(resource.getFile()) which breaks if the resource is inside a JAR (URL-encoded spaces, etc.)
